first_remarks.remarks_to_the_author:
Jiang et al. introduce scGALA, a novel method for cell alignment that can serve as a core module for single-cell data integration. The most notable innovation is that scGALA employs a self-supervised graph link prediction framework combined with a score-based search algorithm to identify high-confidence cell alignments. The authors demonstrate the utility of scGALA across diverse tasks, including batch correction, label transfer, multi-omics integration, spatial data alignment, multiplet-omics integration, cross-modality imputation and spatial transcriptomics enhancement. Overall, scGALA is a versatile and valuable tool for cell alignment-based data integration, with broad applicability to the single-cell data analysis community. However, several major concerns below should be addressed to strengthen the manuscript.

Major comments:

1. It is unclear why the initial inter-dataset edges (MNN- or CCA-based anchors) are combined with the optimized alignment plan P to form the final alignment. Given that the motivation of this work emphasizes limitations of these initial anchors, why keep them in the final result? Would it be possible to only use the optimized alignment plan P as the final alignment? Justification for this design is needed, because suboptimal anchors could compromise cell alignment quality.

2. The link masking procedure lacks critical details. The percentage of links masked is not described in the Methods section (although Fig. 1a suggests 30%). What is the rationale to choose this threshold? A sensitivity analysis should be conducted to demonstrate how varying this hyperparameter affects cell alignment performance.

3. Still for the link masking procedure, are both inter- and intra-dataset edges subject to masking? Given the possible imbalance in edge counts between edge types (e.g., intra- vs. inter-dataset), is random masking appropriate? The authors should clarify whether edge-type-specific masking strategies were considered and justify the uniform strategy.

4. Although scGALA significantly enhances existing cell alignment-based data integration tools (e.g., Seurat), some other top-performing methods, such as Scanorama (Hie, el al., Nature Biotechnology, 2019) for batch effect removal, GLUE (Cao, et al., Nature Biotechnology, 2022) for multi-omics integration and PASTE (Zeira, et al., Nature Methods, 2022) for spatial data alignment, are also deserved to be included in order to strengthen the performance evaluation of scGALA.

5. I was impressed by the capacity of scGALA to improve the gene coverage of spatial transcriptomics data, which would be quite useful in Xenium or MERFISH data analysis. However, the authors only used a simulated sparse dataset to demonstrate its imputation performance. I recommend to apply scGALA to a real Xenium dataset with ground-truth spatial domain annotations. This would further consolidate its applicability to spatial technologies with limited gene throughput.

(Remarks on code availability)

Existing methods identify cell-cell relationships based on rigid feature-wise distance metrics, always missing sufficient and correct cell-cell connections. The authors present a method (scGALA) to enhance this identification, using a graph-based framework. While this paper represents an exciting advancement in single-cell data integration, I do have several concerns that need to be addressed:

## Major:

The authors claim to have proposed a better algorithm for identifying cell-cell relationships. Why don't they directly compare the accuracy of anchor pairs identified by Seurat in Fig. 2?

The batches of scGALA enhanced Seurat-integrated result in Fig. 2a are separated, why have higher ASW batch scores?

In the Results section, the author wrote a lot of summary sentences, such as 'By enabling the integration of multiple doubletomics datasets into …' on page 11. I think most of them should be moved to the Discussion section to increase the clarity of the paper.

The paper lacks a lot of analysis details, which makes it difficult for readers to understand the specific analysis results. Please fill them in the Methods section.

I am a bit confused. scGALA presents itself as an enhanced method for data integration and data transfer, and I don't see results for independent data integration. Why do the authors call it "a standalone integration framework" and "an integration tool"? Or am I missing something? scGALA builds the initial graph in the same way as Conos [1], so why can Conos independently integrate data, but the graph optimized by scGALA cannot? Also, scGALA should be compared with cell-cell relationship identification methods, such as rwMNNs in iMAP framework [2].

The reasons for the selection of the current comparison methods are unclear. Please consider comparing recent unsupervised and supervised integration and data transfer methods, including iMAP, RPCI [3], scPoli [4], and SIGNAL [5].

Please add quantitative indicators such as the accuracy of cell integration in Fig. 4b. It is difficult to conclude from the figure alone that "scGALA's confusion matrices exhibit stronger diagonal enrichment".

Minor:

I think a more general name for "multiplet-omics integration" claimed by the authors is "mosaic integration"[6,7].

There are many typos in the paper. Please revise them thoroughly.

Typo:

Page 2: doublet-omics datasets, triplet-omics;

Page 3: ATAC sequencing data of of 21,178 cells; 10x protocol;

The presentation of Figure 1 is confusing. Please consider reorganizing it.

## Response to Reviewers,

We would like to express our gratitude to the reviewers for their constructive comments and suggestions offered on our manuscript, titled " scGALA: Graph Link Prediction Based Cell Alignment for Comprehensive Data Integration ", with manuscript ID NCOMMS-25-37171A. The detailed feedback has greatly improved the scientific rigor and clarity of the manuscript. Following the guidance provided, we have revised the manuscript accordingly and prepared pointby-point responses addressing all comments. All revisions in the manuscript are marked in blue for easy reference.

## Reviewer #1:

General Comments: Jiang et al. introduce scGALA, a novel method for cell alignment that can serve as a core module for single-cell data integration. The most notable innovation is that scGALA employs a self-supervised graph link prediction framework combined with a score-based search algorithm  to  identify  high-confidence  cell  alignments.  The  authors  demonstrate  the  utility  of scGALA across diverse tasks, including batch correction, label transfer, multi-omics integration, spatial data alignment,  multiplet-omics  integration, cross-modality  imputation  and  spatial transcriptomics enhancement. Overall, scGALA is a versatile and valuable tool for cell alignmentbased  data  integration,  with  broad  applicability  to  the  single-cell  data  analysis  community. However, several major concerns below should be addressed to strengthen the manuscript.

Response: We sincerely thank you for your positive and encouraging feedback on our work. We are particularly grateful for your recognition of scGALA's potential as a versatile and valuable tool with broad applicability for the single-cell data analysis community. We believe scGALA's versatility is demonstrated by its strong performance across a wide range of applications, from batch  correction  and  label  transfer  to  advanced  tasks  such  as  mosaic  integration  and  spatial transcriptomics enhancement. Its broad applicability is further highlighted by its dual functionality as both a powerful standalone framework and a 'plug-in booster' that can enhance numerous stateof-the-art tools, thereby benefiting a wide audience of researchers.

We also appreciate your identification of several major concerns, which have guided our revisions. Specifically, your comments highlighted the need for a clearer justification for combining initial anchors with scGALA's predictions, a more detailed description and sensitivity analysis of the link  masking  procedure,  broader  benchmarking  against  other  top-performing  methods,  and validation of our spatial imputation claims on a real-world, limited-gene-panel dataset.

In response to your comments, we have now performed several new analyses and substantially revised the manuscript:

1. Justification  for  combining  initial  anchors: We  conducted  a  new  ablation  study demonstrating that combining initial high-confidence anchors with  scGALA ' s predictions yields the most accurate and robust alignments. Our results show this combined approach  in  scGALA-enhanced  Seurat  achieves  an  average  label  transfer  accuracy  of 0.8263, a significant improvement over using either initial anchors alone (0.7201) or only the newly predicted links (0.7866). Further details are provided in Comment C1.

2. Link masking procedure: We  added  a  comprehensive  sensitivity  analysis  for  the  link masking hyperparameter and an ablation study comparing different masking strategies. These  analyses  confirm  that  scGALA ' s  performance  is  robust  to  the  masking  ratio (AUROC varying minimally from 0.7526 to 0.7739) and that our default uniform masking strategy  is  the  most  effective  (AUROC  =  0.767),  outperforming  Inter-Only  Masking (0.764) and Intra-Only Masking (0.735). These results provide a clear rationale for our framework ' s design. Please see Comments C2 and C3 for details.
3. Expanded benchmarking: We  have  extended  our  benchmarking  to  include  additional state-of-the-art  methods  such  as  Scanorama  [1],  Conos  [2],  and  STADIA  [3].  scGALA consistently  improves  their  performance;  for  example,  scGALA-enhanced  Scanorama increased biological conservation ARI by 58.04% and the ASW/Batch score by 11.53%, demonstrating its utility as a universal booster. More detailed benchmarking results can be found in Comment C4.
4. Validation on real-world spatial data: We applied scGALA to a Xenium breast cancer dataset [4], confirming its ability to enhance spatial data with high biological fidelity. The imputed  data  improved  spatial  domain  identification ARI  from  0.41  to  0.52,  and  the imputed expression of key marker genes showed a Pearson correlation of 0.96 with groundtruth values, strongly validating its applicability to gene-limited spatial data. Please see Comment C5 for details.

With these additional analyses motivated by your insightful comments, we believe the manuscript has been substantially strengthened.

- C1: It is unclear why the initial inter-dataset edges (MNN- or CCA-based anchors) are combined with the optimized alignment plan P to form the final alignment. Given that the motivation of this work emphasizes limitations of these initial anchors, why keep them in the final result? Would it be possible to only use the optimized alignment plan P as the final alignment? Justification for this design is needed, because suboptimal anchors could compromise cell alignment quality.

Response: We thank you for this insightful question regarding our design choice to combine initial anchors with scGALA's predicted alignments. You raise an important point about the potential for suboptimal  initial  anchors  to  compromise  the  final  alignment.  Our  rationale  is  that  while conventional anchoring methods (e.g., MNN- or CCA-based) have limitations, particularly in their sparsity, they nonetheless provide a set of high-confidence initial matches that serve as an initial scaffold for our graph learning model. Our motivation in developing scGALA was not to discard these  anchors,  but  to  expand  upon  them  systematically  to  achieve  a  more  comprehensive  and accurate  alignment.  Importantly,  scGALA  is  not  dependent  on  anchors  to  function-its  selfsupervised  graph  link  prediction  framework  is  fully  capable  of  identifying  novel  high-quality alignments on its own-but it can leverage anchors when available to maximize robustness.

In light of your concerns, we further investigated this design choice through a newly added ablation study. Following your suggestion, we conducted cell alignment experiments between subsets of

the bone marrow CITE-seq dataset [5] and the PBMC Multiome dataset [6] published by 10X Genomics to compare three strategies: (1) using only initial anchors (MNN), (2) using only the alignments  uniquely  predicted  by  scGALA  ('scGALA  Unique') ,  i.e.,  the  novel  cell  pairs identified exclusively by scGALA and not by conventional anchor methods, and (3) using the combined set ('scGALA').

As  shown  in  Supplementary  Fig.  S23ab,  scGALA  Unique  alignments  constitute  a  substantial fraction (~21%) of the final cell pairings. Importantly, these alignments-discovered exclusively by scGALA-exhibit quality comparable to the initial anchors (average correlation on P5: MNN 0.493; scGALA Unique 0.484), as demonstrated by the similar Spearman correlation distributions of gene expression between aligned cell pairs (Supplementary Fig. S23c-e). This indicates that scGALA successfully enriches the alignment map without sacrificing quality.

Comparable distributions confirm scGALA maintains alignment quality while expanding coverage. f, Label transfer performance

comparison  between  initial  alignments  methods  (CCA  and  MNN),  scGALA  and  scGALA  Unique  alignments, quantified by metrics including accuracy, Cohen's kappa, and 95% confidence intervals.

To further  evaluate  the  impact  of  this  design  choice,  we  compared  downstream  label  transfer performance across the three strategies (Supplementary Fig. S23f), using the same experimental setup  as  in  Fig.  3cd.  The  results  show  that  the  combined  'scGALA'  approach  consistently achieved the highest performance across all metrics in Seurat experiments, with an accuracy of 0.8263 compared to 0.7201 for CCA and 0.7866 for scGALA Unique. In scGCN experiments, the combined approach showed no significant difference from scGALA Unique (P > 0.5), suggesting that anchors are not strictly necessary but can enhance robustness depending on the integration method.  Together,  these  analyses  confirm  that  scGALA  does  not  merely  rely  on  anchors  but extends them with additional high-quality alignments to yield the most comprehensive results.

We  acknowledge  that  these  ablations  were  performed  on  a  representative  dataset,  and  while preliminary tests on additional tissues show similar trends, the magnitude of improvement may vary depending on dataset properties. To provide transparency and flexibility, we updated the GitHub repository to include an optional mode that allows users to exclude initial anchors from the final output (via replace=True in the get\_alignment function).

In summary, scGALA introduces a self-supervised graph link prediction framework coupled with a score-based search strategy for cell alignment. Initial anchors provide a sparse but highconfidence scaffold, and scGALA enriches this with novel alignments of comparable quality that conventional methods  cannot  recover. The  combined  strategy  achieves the most  robust performance, but scGALA remains effective as a standalone method. The ability to function both with  and  without  anchors  demonstrates  that  scGALA's  booster  property  arises  from  its  novel framework, rather than from reliance on conventional anchors.

- C2: The  link  masking  procedure  lacks  critical  details.  The  percentage  of  links  masked  is  not described in the Methods section (although Fig. 1a suggests 30%). What is the rationale to choose this  threshold?  A  sensitivity  analysis  should  be  conducted  to  demonstrate  how  varying  this hyperparameter affects cell alignment performance.

Response: We thank you for pointing out this lack of clarity. The link masking ratio is indeed a key hyperparameter. As per your suggestion, we have now clarified the link masking procedure in the "Methods" section. Additionally, we added a new sensitivity analysis to justify our choice of the masking ratio.

To provide a clearer understanding of how this hyperparameter functions within our framework, we detail the self-supervised approach we employed. In our self-supervised framework, a fraction of edges in the graph is randomly hidden (masked) at each training step, and the model is trained to  predict  these  masked  edges.  We  selected  a  default  masking  ratio  of  30%  as  it  provides  a sufficient number of edges for both robust training and effective validation. As per your suggestion, to  formally  assess  the  impact  of  this  hyperparameter,  we  conducted  a  sensitivity  analysis  by varying the masking ratio from 20% to 50%.

The results, now included in Supplementary Fig. S20, demonstrate that scGALA's performance is robust against varying masking ratios. The ROC curves for each ratio are nearly overlapping, with

AUROC values showing  minimal  variation  (from  0.755  to  0.767;  Supplementary  Fig.  S20a), confirming  the  robustness  of  our  approach  to  this  hyperparameter.  This  stability  is  further supported by the cell type-specific confusion matrices in Supplementary Fig. S20b, which show strong diagonal enrichment and consistently accurate alignments regardless of the masking ratio. While  a  ratio  of  30%  yielded  a  marginally  higher  average  AUROC  of  0.767,  the  overall performance is robust to the choice of masking ratio. We have now included these details and the rationale in the "Methods" section.

C3: Still for the link masking procedure, are both inter- and intra-dataset edges subject to masking? Given the possible imbalance in edge counts between edge types (e.g., intra- vs. inter-dataset), is random  masking  appropriate?  The  authors  should  clarify  whether  edge-type-specific  masking strategies were considered and justify the uniform strategy.

Response: We thank you for this insightful question about the edge type considered in our masking strategy. In our current implementation, we apply a uniform random masking strategy to both intraand inter-dataset edges. The rationale for masking intra-dataset edges is that it encourages the model  to  learn  robust  representations  of  cell  identity  and  neighborhood  structure.  Given  that single-cell data often suffers from dropout, intra-dataset edges can be noisy or missing. By training the model to reconstruct these connections, we improve the quality of the cell embeddings, which in turn enhances the model's ability to predict correct inter-dataset alignments.

To  further  investigate  the  effectiveness  of  this  approach,  we  performed  an  ablation  study  to validate this uniform strategy by comparing it against two alternatives: 1) masking only interdataset edges ("Inter-Only") and 2) masking only intra-dataset edges ("Intra-Only"). The results are  now  presented  in  the  new  Supplementary  Fig.  S21.  The  ROC  curves  and  corresponding AUROC scores in Supplementary Fig. S21ab show that the Uniform (AUROC: 0.767) and InterOnly (AUROC: 0.764) masking strategies perform comparably and are both superior to the IntraOnly  (AUROC:  0.735)  strategy.  We  believe  that  the  Intra-Only  approach  has  some  limited effectiveness because information flow within the graph can indirectly refine embeddings and help predict  some  new inter-dataset  edges.  However,  this  strategy  can  be  handicapped  when  initial intra-dataset edges are themselves inaccurate, which is a common issue in sparse datasets with high dropout.

Then, compared with Inter-Only Masking, the slight advantage of the Uniform approach suggests that learning to reconstruct the intra-dataset graph provides valuable information that refines cell embeddings. The KDE plot in Supplementary Fig. S21c reveals that all three strategies identify new  alignments  of  comparable  quality,  as  indicated  by  their  similar  Spearman  correlation distributions (average correlation: Uniform Masking 0.496; Inter-Only Masking 0.507; Intra-Only Masking 0.498). Finally, the confusion matrices in Supplementary Fig. S21d visually confirm the quantitative results, with the Uniform and Inter-Only strategies yielding clearer diagonal patterns than the Intra-Only approach.

These results, showing the superior performance of Uniform masking, support our choice of a uniform masking strategy as the default.  We have added this analysis to the supplement and now discuss the rationale for our uniform masking strategy in the Methods section. Recognizing the value of flexibility where the intra- or inter-dataset relationship may be considered more valuable, we have updated our software to allow users to input the weight for weighted masking strategy in get\_alignment function, enabling them to specify different masking probabilities for intra- and inter-dataset edges if desired for specific applications.

C4: Although scGALA significantly enhances existing cell alignment-based data integration tools (e.g.,  Seurat),  some  other  top-performing  methods,  such  as  Scanorama  (Hie,  el  al.,  Nature Biotechnology, 2019) for batch effect removal, GLUE (Cao, et al., Nature Biotechnology, 2022) for  multi-omics  integration  and  PASTE  (Zeira,  et  al.,  Nature  Methods,  2022)  for  spatial  data alignment, are also deserved to be included in order to strengthen the performance evaluation of scGALA.

Response: We thank you for this excellent suggestion to broaden our benchmarking against other top-performing  methods.  We  agree  with  you  that  a  comprehensive  comparison  is  essential  to position scGALA within the current landscape of integration tools.

As per your suggestion, we have expanded our benchmarks to include: Seurat [7] (unsupervised), INSCT [8] (in both supervised and unsupervised modes), scDML [9] (unsupervised), Scanorama [1] (unsupervised, newly added), iMAP [10]  (unsupervised, newly added), and STACAS [11] (semi-supervised, newly added) in our batch correction benchmarks; Seurat, scGCN [12], Conos [2],  and Monet [13]  (newly  added)  for  label  transfer.  For  multi-omics  integration  and  spatial alignment, we carefully considered all suggested methods. However, GLUE [14] and PASTE [15] are  not  directly  comparable  since  they  lack  an  intermediate  cell-cell  alignment  module  that scGALA  could  replace  or  augment.  GLUE  performs  integration  via  modeling  the  regulatory interactions across omics layers explicitly as a guidance graph, and PASTE performs slice-level alignment  directly using the iterative conditional gradient algorithm. While  not  directly comparable, we see GLUE and PASTE as complementary rather than competing frameworks, as they represent alternative approaches that do not rely on direct cell-cell alignments. Therefore, to provide a fair and relevant comparison against other state-of-the-art alignment-based tools, we have instead included scCross [16], GCN-SC [17], Seurat, and Conos [2] (newly added) for multiomics integration; STAligner [18], INSCT, Seurat, and STADIA [3]  (newly added) for spatial alignment in our expanded benchmark analysis. These benchmarks of newly added methods are conducted on the same datasets as in Fig. 3.

The  results  of  this  expanded  evaluation  are  presented  in  Supplementary  Fig.  S3.  For  batch correction,  the  UMAP visualizations  in  Supplementary  Fig.  S3a  show  that  scGALA-enhanced Scanorama  produces  more  coherent  cell  type  clusters  with  better  mixing  of  batches.  This  is quantitatively supported in Supplementary Fig. S3b, which shows significant improvements in biological  conservation metrics (e.g. improve Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) [19] by 58.04% for Scanorama) for all tested methods, including Scanorama, iMAP, and STACAS. For label transfer, Supplementary Fig.  S3c  and  Supplementary  Fig.  S3d  demonstrate  that  enhancing  Monet  with scGALA leads to more accurate cell type predictions, improving Kappa score by 5.8%. In multi-

omics integration, Supplementary Fig. S3ef show that scGALA-enhanced Conos improves the alignment of RNA and ATAC modalities, resulting in more integrated domain mixing with a 24.4% improvement in ASW/Domain score, and lower FOSCTTM [20] scores with a 48.0% decrease, indicating a more accurate correspondence between paired cells. Finally, for spatial alignment, Supplementary Fig. S3gh reveal that scGALA-enhanced STADIA achieves more precise matching of spatial domains across tissue slices, reflected by the increase in alignment accuracy by 4.9%.

This expanded benchmarking reinforces scGALA's utility as a universal enhancer for a wide range of alignment-based integration methods. These results have been incorporated into the Results section of the manuscript.

C5: I  was  impressed  by  the  capacity  of  scGALA  to  improve  the  gene  coverage  of  spatial transcriptomics  data,  which  would  be  quite  useful  in  Xenium  or  MERFISH  data  analysis. However,  the  authors  only  used  a  simulated  sparse  dataset  to  demonstrate  its  imputation performance. I recommend to apply scGALA to a real Xenium dataset with ground-truth spatial domain annotations. This would further consolidate its applicability to spatial technologies with limited gene throughput.

Response: We thank you for this valuable suggestion and for recognizing the capacity of scGALA to improve the gene coverage of spatial transcriptomics data. scGALA effectively addresses the issue of limited gene panels of spatially resolved transcriptomics technologies like Xenium by using a reference scRNA-seq dataset to impute missing expression, expanding gene coverage over three-fold while preserving spatial organization. To make sure there is ground truth to compare with, we evaluated this function on simulated datasets with genes sampled from a Visium dataset. We agree that experiment on a real Xenium dataset with ground-truth spatial domain annotations would greatly consolidate the applicability of scGALA to spatial technologies with limited gene throughput.

Following your recommendation, we have now applied scGALA to a real-world Xenium human breast cancer dataset [4], which has a limited panel of 541 genes and is accompanied by groundtruth spatial domain annotations.
